product: Residential fiber internet (standalone, no bundled mobile plan or TV bundle)
region: Leesburg and Mount Dora, Lake County, FL
segment: Budget-conscious and value-seeking residential households, in two sub-segments assigned by primary barrier to switching: cost-constrained households (affordability of getting or staying connected) and value switchers (already subscribed; post-promo bill increases, switching friction, trust)

customer_segments.name: Cost-constrained households
customer_segments.definition: The barrier is affording to get or stay connected: monthly price, upfront costs (install, equipment, deposits), credit checks and contract lock-in. Commonly renters, multifamily residents, and households affected by the end of the Affordable Connectivity Program.

customer_segments.name: Value switchers
customer_segments.definition: Already subscribed; the barrier is switching friction and trust in a new provider, and the trigger is the bill increase after promotional pricing expires. Commonly homeowners, including retirees and manufactured-home owners. They value reliability and simple, predictable billing.

segment_rule: Assign households by their primary barrier to switching, not by age or income source: a fixed-income or retired household belongs to whichever segment matches its primary barrier.
business_question: Given that Wire3 cannot compete on mobile or TV bundling or on brand recognition, what go-to-market strategy (positioning, pricing and promo structure, affordability options, messaging, channels) will convert budget-conscious and value-seeking households in Leesburg and Mount Dora away from Xfinity, CenturyLink, Quantum Fiber, Spectrum, T-Mobile Home Internet and Verizon Home Internet, within budget?
research_questions: What is each competitor's serviceable footprint and advertised speed tiers in Leesburg and Mount Dora, and where does each overlap with Wire3's publicly listed coverage?
What are each competitor's current standalone and bundled pricing tiers, promo rates, and post-promo rates?
What upfront and recurring costs does each competitor charge (install, equipment, deposits or credit checks, early-termination fees, data caps and overages, surcharges)?

What low-income, prepaid, or no-contract options does each competitor offer (e.g. Xfinity Internet Essentials, Xfinity NOW, Lifeline-eligible plans), and what changed for households after the Affordable Connectivity Program ended?

What public demographic and housing data describes Leesburg and Mount Dora (income, poverty, renters vs. owners, multifamily and manufactured housing, age, broadband adoption, languages), at city-limit and ZIP level?
What documented triggers cause residential customers to switch ISPs (promo-cliff bill shock, reliability, customer service, moving)?
How much do mobile and TV bundles influence purchase decisions for budget-conscious households compared with other segments?
What do verified customer reviews and complaints say about each competitor's pain points, prioritizing Lake County and Central Florida sources?
How have regional fiber ISPs without a mobile bundle positioned and priced against a cable incumbent, including affordable tiers, community partnerships and apartment programs?

Which marketing channels are effective and cost-appropriate for a low-awareness regional ISP entering Lake County neighborhoods (community groups, libraries, property and manufactured-home community managers, local media, direct mail, geo-targeted digital, referrals)?
Which local organizations active in digital inclusion or affordability in Lake County could be credible partners?
research_question_priority: RQ1-RQ4 first, then RQ5, then RQ9-RQ10, then the rest
required_output_sections: Risks, assumptions, and open follow-up research questions

preferred: Lake County and city government sites
Wayback Machine snapshots of provider pages (via its API)
excluded: crime statistics as a basis for targeting or excluding neighborhoods
FCC National Broadband Map web interface

framing_rules: Describe neighborhoods and households only by publicly measurable economic and connectivity characteristics; never by crime, safety or other stigmatizing descriptors.
Never recommend excluding, deprioritizing or offering worse terms to areas based on income or demographic composition.

Only facts from Wire3's public website are real Wire3 inputs; everything else about Wire3 must not be guessed. If Wire3 lists no affordability plan, one may be recommended as a hypothetical but never stated to exist.
All pricing, promo, spend and channel recommendations are hypothetical and illustrative for an academic capstone, not Wire3's actual plan.
compliance_considerations: FCC broadband consumer labels: any advertised plan must show its monthly price, promo terms, one-time and recurring fees, and speeds in the FCC label format.
Promotional and post-promo pricing claims must be clear and not misleading under the FTC Act and the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act.

FCC rules on digital discrimination of access (47 CFR Part 16): check their current status and whether deployment, pricing or service decisions differ by income, race, ethnicity, color, religion or national origin.
Affordability programs: do not state or imply that Wire3 participates in Lifeline or any subsidy program unless its public website says so; the Affordable Connectivity Program has ended.
Property-manager and manufactured-home community agreements: check that exclusive-access or bulk-billing terms comply with FCC rules for multiple-tenant environments.
